title: Nodal nematic superconductivity in moiré graphene
authors: Shuwen Sun, Grgur Palle, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Rafael M. Fernandes, Pablo Jarillo-Herrero, Jeong Min Park
abstract: Unconventional superconductivity can emerge in various forms in strongly correlated systems. Historically, the most extensively studied examples include nodal and triplet pairing, which were experimentally detected in cuprates and superfluid helium-3, respectively. Beyond these canonical cases, there are also nematic superconductors, in which the rotational symmetry of the lattice is broken in the superconducting state. While there are several examples of nematic superconductors whose pairing emerges inside a preexisting nematic normal state, experimental evidence for superconducting states that intrinsically break rotational symmetry on their own has been exceedingly scarce. Here, we report the experimental realization and identification of an intrinsic multi-component nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (MATTG). By integrating tunneling spectroscopy with quantum transport measurements, we directly probe the symmetry of low-energy superconducting quasiparticles. Deep inside the superconducting state, we observe a pronounced two-fold anisotropy in the zero-bias tunneling conductance under an in-plane magnetic field, which is strongly suppressed together with superconductivity as the temperature or perpendicular magnetic field is increased. Remarkably, the major axis of anisotropy rotates by up to $90^{\circ}$ across the superconducting dome, indicating an intrinsic, field- and density-tunable symmetry of the low-energy excitations. These behaviors imply a nodal superconducting state in MATTG that spontaneously breaks the six-fold rotational symmetry of the moiré superlattice. Our results establish moiré graphene as a versatile platform for realizing and interrogating nodal nematic superconductivity, opening a new avenue for exploring unconventional symmetry-breaking superconducting states in two-dimensional materials.
summary: This work reports the experimental discovery of a nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene. By measuring the angular dependence of the superconducting gap via tunneling spectroscopy, the authors observe a characteristic two-fold anisotropy. This finding establishes moiré graphene as a tunable platform for studying unconventional, symmetry-breaking superconductivity.
main_problem: The paper reports the experimental realization and identification of an intrinsic multi-component nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (MATTG).
main_result: The observation of a pronounced, field-tunable two-fold anisotropy in the zero-bias tunneling conductance, which rotates across the superconducting dome, confirms the existence of a nodal nematic superconducting state.
method: The study integrates tunneling spectroscopy and quantum transport measurements to directly probe the symmetry of low-energy superconducting quasiparticles.
model_or_system: The physical system is Magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (MATTG), a moiré superlattice known for hosting unconventional superconductivity. The analysis focuses on probing the symmetry breaking in the superconducting state.
key_observables: Zero-bias tunneling conductance (dI/dV) under an in-plane magnetic field, anisotropy ratio ($\eta$), and temperature/field dependence of these measurements.
important_parameters: Low-energy superconducting gap ($\sim 0.1$ meV), in-plane magnetic field ($B_{\|}$), temperature ($T$), and doping/gate voltage ($V_{	ext{BG}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the observed anisotropy is intrinsically linked to the superconducting pairing symmetry, and that the dominant symmetry breaking is related to the in-plane d-vector.
figures_summary: Figures show device characterization (transport/tunneling), the angular dependence of the zero-bias conductance revealing two-fold anisotropy, and the suppression of this anisotropy with increasing temperature or perpendicular magnetic field.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by characterizing the superconducting state using transport and tunneling measurements, identifying the two-fold anisotropy as a key signature, and then theoretically linking this signature to a nodal nematic pairing symmetry.
why_interesting: The direct experimental measurement of symmetry breaking in the superconducting gap structure provides a concrete platform for testing theoretical models of unconventional pairing symmetries in 2D correlated electron systems.
